articles.title: I have a wild theory about the 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' post-credits scene — here's how I think it sets up a big surprise in Avengers: Doomsday
articles.text:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day's post-credits scene might not mean what you think it does — here's my wild theory about the new Marvel movie's final shot
Spider-Man: Brand New Day has spun its way into theaters — and there's something about the Marvel movie's end credits scene that's dominated my thoughts since I left my screening.
I've already written about the post-credits stinger in my Spider-Man: Brand New Day ending explained piece, but I didn't elaborate on what it could be teasing. That's because, based on a new theory I have about this Spider-Man film's end credits scene, I deemed that discussion worthy of its own article.
It goes without saying, but full spoilers immediately follow for Spider-Man: Brand New Day. If you haven't seen it yet: bookmark this page, read my Spider-Man: Brand New Day review to see if it's any good, and then watch it at your local theater. Once you've completed those steps, re-open this page — it'll be worth the wait, I promise.
Alright, let's first review what happens in Spider-Man 4's post-credits scene, which centers on the Spidey Tracker app developed by Ned Leeds.
Initially, a flashing marker, accompanied by an automated voice message that says "New Spider-Man sighting", indicates that the titular hero is still in New York City. However, the message soon starts saying "Location unknown", which highlights that Spider-Man's actual whereabouts are, well, unknown. Cue the app zooming out to try to find Peter Parker.
Eventually, the app zooms out far enough that it not only shows us the entire Earth, but also that the popular Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) character can't be found. That's until the app moves away from our world, lays down a new pin that indicates Spider-Man is somewhere in space, and ends with the voice message saying "Location found."
What does that mean? The obvious answer is that Spidey is no longer planet-side. I know, shock, horror. What isn't clear, though, is why he's in space. Again, there's an easy answer for this: it's got something to do with Avengers: Doomsday and/or its sequel Avengers: Secret Wars.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
That pair, which come out on December 18, 2026 and December 17, 2027, mark the end of Marvel Phase 6 and the divisive Marvel Multiverse Saga. And, while current Spidey star Tom Holland isn't confirmed to appear in Doomsday, the fan-favorite A-lister will, by virtue of his popularity, feature in one or both of the aforementioned films. So, it would make a ton of sense if Brand New Day's end credits stinger is teasing his involvement in Doomsday and/or Secret Wars.
Nonetheless, what if — and I realize this is a huge if — the Spidey Tracker isn't picking up Holland's Spider-Man, but one of his fellow webheads?
Now, I know that's a stretch, but hear me out. After all, everything we learn about the Spidey Tracker in Brand New Day suggests it's tailored specifically to the MCU's Spider-Man, so why would it detect another wallcrawler, such as Tobey Maguire or Andrew Garfield's, instead?
Well, for one, we don't actually know that the Spidey Tracker has been custom-built for Holland's version. If it hasn't, there's no reason why it wouldn't detect one of his multiversal variants.
That multiversal aspect is perhaps the most crucial part of my theory, too.
The next two Avengers movies will be the culmination — and celebration — of every Marvel Universe we've seen on the big screen. That includes the MCU, the original Fox X-Men franchise, and — based on myriad rumors that have been circulating online for months — the realities inhabited by Maguire and Garfield.
Furthermore, Avengers: Doomsday's story synopsis has already confirmed that it'll revolve around the threat posed by Incursions.
These multiversal calamities occur when the barriers between two universes break down, and lead to a collision that permanently destroys one or both worlds. As such, Doomsday will feature heroes from three distinct universes — the MCU, original FoX-Men, and The Fantastic Four — battling to save their realities.
But are these the only universes we'll visit in Avengers 5? It would be a glaring error if Marvel overlooked Maguire and Garfield's worlds in Doomsday and/or Secret Wars, and I don't think anyone believes that the comic giant would.
It's for that very reason, then, that I believe Brand New Day's post-credits scene isn't actually showing us that Holland's Parker has gone off-world. No, I'm convinced that the Spidey Tracker is actually picking up Maguire or Garfield's Spider-Man — and, of the two, it's the former that it's detected.
Think about it. Doomsday's first proper trailer appears to suggest that the FoX-Men have successfully navigated an Incursion. I speculate more on this in my Avengers: Doomsday trailer breakdown article, but essentially, the teaser's first few seconds show Charles Xavier/Professor X shielding his eyes from a humungous, blinding explosion. Of course, this might not be the final moments of the FoX-Men destroying another world to save their own, but what else could cause such a massive and bright blast if not the destruction of an entire universe?
And what's that got to do with Maguire's Spider-Man? Well, maybe it's his reality — aka the Sam Raimi Spider-Verse — that's being annihilated in that scene. If so, it's possible that a giant mega-Incursion involving the MCU, Fantastic Four-Verse, FoX-Men universe, and Raimi-Verse happens at the same time in Doomsday, which results in the FoX-Men proactively destroying the Raimi-Verse because their reality is most at risk of colliding with it.
Should that be the case, it would explain why the Spidey Tracker detects Maguire's Peter Parker instead of Holland's and subsequently backs up my admittedly wild theory.
There's the tiniest shred of evidence that I might be onto something, too. During a cute chat with kids on the Celebrity Surprise YouTube channel, Holland was asked if Maguire would appear in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Holland's reply? "He's not in the movie [Spider-Man 4], but... yeah, I... yeah, careful now."
The implication here is that Holland knows something about when and where Maguire's version of the character could show up next. Holland is famous for having loose lips when it comes to MCU spoilers, too, so the fact that he stops himself here before he reveals something is, in itself, revealing.
Does he know that Maguire will feature in Doomsday and/or Secret Wars? I wouldn't be shocked if he does. After all, Holland, Maguire, and Garfield all shared the screen in 2021's Spider-Man: No Way Home. If they still keep in touch, it's plausible they've discussed their possible involvement in one or both forthcoming Avengers films, with Maguire potentially telling them — in the strictest confidence — that he's in Avengers: Doomsday. For the sake of my offbeat theory, I hope that's the case.
In the meantime, learn everything we know so far about Avengers: Doomsday, get the lowdown on Avengers: Secret Wars, and find out how to watch the Marvel movies in order.

articles.title: Google prepara Pixel Tag para encontrar objetos perdidos: le llegó competencia al AirTag de Apple
articles.text:
Google estaría a punto de entrar de lleno en el mercado de los localizadores inteligentes con el desarrollo del Pixel Tag, un accesorio diseñado para ayudar a encontrar llaves, mochilas, maletas y otros objetos personales mediante la red Find Hub. Aunque la compañía aún no ha anunciado oficialmente el dispositivo, una reciente filtración mostró su diseño y reveló algunos detalles sobre su funcionamiento.
El Pixel Tag aprovecharía la infraestructura de Find Hub, anteriormente conocida como Find My Device, para localizar objetos perdidos utilizando la extensa red de dispositivos Android.
PUBLICIDAD
La filtración llega a pocos días del evento Made by Google, programado para el 12 de agosto de 2026, donde la empresa ya confirmó la presentación de la nueva familia Pixel 11. El rastreador podría convertirse en una de las principales sorpresas del evento.
Hasta ahora, Google había fortalecido Find Hub para localizar teléfonos, auriculares y otros accesorios compatibles, pero aún carecía de un producto propio que compitiera directamente con el AirTag de Apple. Todo indica que esa situación podría cambiar muy pronto.
PUBLICIDAD
La primera imagen deja ver un diseño compacto y redondeado
Las imágenes filtradas por 9to5Google muestran un dispositivo pequeño, con bordes redondeados y un aspecto diferente al AirTag. Mientras el accesorio de Apple mantiene un formato completamente circular, el supuesto Pixel Tag presenta una silueta ligeramente ovalada, alineada con el diseño habitual de otros productos Pixel.
Aunque todavía no existen especificaciones oficiales, el dispositivo parece pensado para transportarse fácilmente junto a objetos cotidianos como llaves, equipaje, carteras o mochilas.
Uno de los aspectos que todavía genera dudas es si incluirá un orificio para sujetarlo directamente a un llavero. Esta característica ha sido una de las solicitudes más repetidas por los usuarios del AirTag, ya que el accesorio de Apple requiere una funda adicional para poder engancharse.
PUBLICIDAD
La filtración tampoco permite confirmar el tipo de batería, el peso, el tamaño exacto ni los materiales utilizados en su fabricación.
Find Hub será la pieza clave del sistema
El funcionamiento del Pixel Tag estaría basado en Find Hub, la plataforma de localización de Google que utiliza millones de dispositivos Android repartidos por todo el mundo.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuando un teléfono Android detecta mediante Bluetooth un rastreador perdido, puede enviar de forma cifrada su ubicación aproximada al propietario. Todo el proceso ocurre automáticamente y sin que la persona que lleva el teléfono conozca la identidad del dueño del accesorio.
Este sistema funciona de manera similar al ecosistema Buscar de Apple, que aprovecha la enorme cantidad de iPhone activos para localizar AirTags incluso cuando se encuentran lejos de su propietario.
PUBLICIDAD
En teoría, Android dispone de una base de dispositivos aún mayor. Sin embargo, Google ha enfrentado durante años el reto de ofrecer una experiencia homogénea debido a la enorme diversidad de fabricantes, configuraciones de privacidad y accesorios compatibles.
La llegada de un dispositivo propio permitiría a la compañía controlar tanto el hardware como el software, optimizando la experiencia de búsqueda.
Un producto que puede fortalecer el ecosistema Pixel
Actualmente existen diversos localizadores compatibles con Find Hub fabricados por empresas como Motorola, Chipolo o Pebblebee.
Cada uno ofrece características diferentes, desde baterías reemplazables hasta diseños específicos para equipaje o llaveros. Sin embargo, ninguno pertenece directamente a Google.
Con el Pixel Tag, la empresa podría establecer un estándar dentro de Android, del mismo modo que los teléfonos Pixel sirven como referencia para mostrar las capacidades más recientes del sistema operativo.
PUBLICIDAD
Esto facilitaría una integración más profunda con los teléfonos Pixel y posiblemente con otros dispositivos del ecosistema, ofreciendo una configuración más sencilla y una experiencia uniforme para los usuarios.
Además, disponer de un producto propio permitiría a Google impulsar más rápidamente las mejoras en Find Hub, incorporando nuevas funciones conforme evolucione la plataforma.
Apple sigue siendo el principal rival
Desde su lanzamiento, el AirTag se convirtió en uno de los localizadores inteligentes más populares del mercado gracias a su integración con la aplicación Buscar y la enorme red de dispositivos Apple.
PUBLICIDAD
Su éxito impulsó a otros fabricantes a desarrollar productos similares compatibles con Android, aunque hasta ahora Google había optado por limitarse al desarrollo de la plataforma de localización.
La aparición del Pixel Tag supone un cambio de estrategia. En lugar de depender exclusivamente de terceros, la compañía podría ofrecer una solución completamente integrada dentro de su ecosistema.
PUBLICIDAD
Esta decisión también responde al creciente interés de los consumidores por dispositivos capaces de localizar objetos personales de forma rápida, especialmente durante viajes o desplazamientos cotidianos.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Do you support banning phones in schools? A new poll suggests 77% of adults are now in favor of a classroom ban
articles.text:
Do you support banning phones in schools? A new poll suggests 77% of adults are now in favor of a classroom ban
TechRadar readers can vote and make their opinions known here
Banning phones in schools. Yay or nay? It's certainly a topic that's raised debate on both sides in recent years as more states look to enforce stricter rules. Interestingly, however, it does appear that public opinion is starting to sway heavily towards the 'pro ban' camp.
A new report from the Pew Research Center has just concluded that an overwhelming 77 percent of adults surveyed now support a ban on phones in the classroom. That's a massive increase from the 36 percent reported just two years ago.
The ban on phones in the classroom is generally considered distinct from a full ban on devices in schools - commonly referred to as a 'bell-to-bell' ban. Support for a full ban remains firmly split in the Pew report, with 48 percent of adults supporting a full ban in comparison.
Teachers have long been overwhelming advocates of stricter rules. A 2024 survey by the National Education Association found that a whopping 90 percent of teachers supported a ban on phones in class, whereas this 2025 survey by RAND found that 70 percent of school principals believe bans have a positive effect in school. Now, however, it appears that the general public is increasingly on board.
But what do you think? At TechRadar, we're interested in hearing what our readers have to say. I've attached a poll just down below, and we'd also love to hear your concerns in the comments, if you have any.
Do you support a phone ban in the classroom?
The case for a ban
- Studies have suggested an improvement in suspension rates
- Evidence for improved performance is more mixed
On a gut level, it certainly feels like phones should be out of the classroom. As adults, we're increasingly recognizing the perceived downsides of doomscrolling, social media, or other common phone-based habits. I know I've certainly felt frustrated at my own tendency to be distracted by my phone during work hours.
Luckily, we don't have to just rely on gut feeling; however, as there is in fact some evidence to suggest that phone bans in schools result in better outcomes for students.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Perhaps the most convincing report I've seen is from the Education Next Journal, which collated evidence from Florida's state-wide ban in 2023. While other states have followed suit, Florida is a particularly good case as it was the first state to actually institute a ban. In short, the data is strong here.
Interestingly, the report suggests a higher suspension rate in the first year of the ban, followed by a return to a base level, followed by an overall decrease. Test scores remained steady in the year after the ban but then massively improved in the second year. That suggests it takes a while for any positive changes to be evident.
Another excellent report is from the National Bureau of Economic Research, which studied students from 40,000 schools nationwide between 2019 and 2025. In this study, students reported a greater sense of well-being post-ban as well as decreased suspension rates long-term (after a temporary increase).
This report's findings are a little less cut-and-dry than Education Next's, however, as it didn't find any meaningful effects on test scores. Overall, the report still skews toward viewing a ban favorably, and crucially reports on students' own sense of well-being.
The case against a ban
- Parents cite child safety as a concern
- Questions remain around other tech devices
So are there any arguments against a ban? Well, the answer is actually yes; there are a few, and they're mostly fielded by concerned parents.
The most common point I've seen raised is the issue of safety in schools. Some have commented that they'd prefer for their child to have a phone in the case of an emergency on school grounds.
Even though I don't have kids, I can certainly empathize with parents in this case. Sadly, we know that violence continues to be an issue in schools, so it's a very good point that absolutely shouldn't be ignored when exploring this topic.
One other point that I've seen raised, and one that certainly also holds weight, is that even with a phone ban, children may still be distracted by other forms of technology in the classroom. If a child still has a laptop, for example, then they may still have access to social media, messaging, and so on.
This was actually suggested by the authors of the National Bureau of Economic Research report as one of the reasons why test results didn't improve in their study. Certainly, it could suggest that you really need a holistic approach to technology as a whole in the classroom. Banning smartphones could just be the start.

articles.title: Qué pasa si contesto una llamada spam y digo “si”
articles.text:
El teléfono suena. El número es desconocido, pero se atiende igual. Del otro lado, una voz grabada o un silencio breve antes de que alguien hable. Es una llamada spam: una comunicación no solicitada cuyo objetivo es obtener dinero o información personal del receptor.
Según datos de la empresa de ciberseguridad Kaspersky, hasta el 70% de las llamadas de números desconocidos provienen de estafadores, y la cantidad de números no deseados en su base de datos se multiplicó por seis desde 2020.
PUBLICIDAD
La pregunta que pocos se hacen antes de colgar es qué consecuencias tiene haber atendido, y qué pasa si durante esa llamada se dijo “sí”.
Qué ocurre cuando se atiende una llamada spam
Contestar una llamada de spam, aunque sea por error, tiene una consecuencia inmediata: confirma a los cibercriminales que el número está activo y pertenece a una persona real.
PUBLICIDAD
Así lo advierten expertos de la firma de ciberseguridad Keeper Security: a partir de ese momento, el usuario pasa a ser un objetivo preferente para fraudes y manipulaciones, y la frecuencia de nuevos intentos aumenta.
Durante la llamada, los estafadores suelen intentar obtener datos personales, simular la identidad de bancos o instituciones oficiales, o presionar a la víctima para que realice algún pago.
PUBLICIDAD
Las técnicas más habituales incluyen mensajes pregrabados, amenazas con supuestos cargos o sanciones y promesas de premios inexistentes. La urgencia y la intimidación son los recursos psicológicos centrales: buscan que la víctima actúe sin pensar.
En los casos más sofisticados, los ciberdelincuentes graban la voz del usuario durante la conversación y la emplean en ataques de vishing: con herramientas de inteligencia artificial, generan imitaciones de esa voz para suplantar la identidad de la víctima ante familiares o contactos.
PUBLICIDAD
Las consecuencias pueden incluir robo de identidad, transferencias bancarias no autorizadas y daños a la reputación financiera y legal del afectado. Las entidades legítimas no pedirán información sensible en llamadas entrantes.
Por qué decir “sí” agrava el riesgo
Responder “sí” durante una llamada spam no es un gesto neutral. Los estafadores pueden grabar esa palabra y utilizarla para simular un consentimiento verbal: autorizar cargos, activar suscripciones o validar transacciones presentando la grabación como prueba de acuerdo por parte de la víctima.
PUBLICIDAD
A eso se suma el riesgo de la clonación de voz.
Una sola sílaba grabada puede ser suficiente para que los sistemas de inteligencia artificial procesen la muestra y generen una imitación utilizable en nuevos fraudes: llamadas a familiares solicitando dinero de urgencia o intentos de acceso a plataformas bancarias que verifican identidad por voz.
PUBLICIDAD
Según Keeper Security, la respuesta correcta ante cualquier llamada sospechosa es no interactuar: colgar de inmediato, bloquear el número y reportarlo ante las autoridades correspondientes, como la Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones (FCC) en Estados Unidos o el organismo equivalente en cada país.
Cualquier palabra pronunciada (“sí“, “hola” o el propio nombre) es suficiente para que los sistemas automatizados registren el número como activo y escalen la intensidad de los ataques futuros.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo silenciar las llamadas de desconocidos
El proceso para silenciar las llamadas de desconocidos es:
- En iPhone: ve a Configuración, toca Apps y luego Teléfono. Busca la opción de Silenciar desconocidos y actívala. Las llamadas de números que no están en tus contactos se redirigen directamente al buzón de voz.
- En Android (con la app de Teléfono de Google): ve a Más opciones > Configuración > Identificador de llamada y spam, y activa “Ver ID de emisor y spam”. Para un filtro más estricto, activa también “Filtrar llamadas de spam”: las llamadas bloqueadas no generan notificación, pero quedan registradas en el historial y el buzón de voz.
Instalar una aplicación de filtrado de terceros agrega una capa extra de protección.
Estas apps se basan en bases de datos de números de spam conocidos y, en muchos casos, incorporan retroalimentación de usuarios e inteligencia artificial para identificar números fraudulentos en tiempo real.

articles.title: Insta360's new device just changed how I shoot POV footage — and it's not even a camera
articles.text:
Insta360's new device solves the biggest problem with first-person video — and it’s not a camera
Hands-free POV filming just got a whole lot easier
- New accessory for Luna Ultra synchronizes the camera with the user's head movement
- POV Head Tracker simplifies shooting hands-free first-person footage
- It costs $69.99 / £67.99 / AU$115.99
Do you ever shoot first-person-view (FPV) video content? Well, Insta360 has a new accessory that's designed to simplify the whole experience: the POV Head Tracker. And it might just tempt you to switch to the Luna Ultra.
The coin-sized 0.2oz / 6.4g device connects to the Luna Ultra compact vlogging camera over Bluetooth and, once paired, it synchronizes the camera with your head movement in real time, for what Insta360 says is "immersive POV footage".
It's designed to completely free up your hands, but goes one step further than a simple chest mount by synchronizing head and camera movement, so you shouldn't have to worry at all about composing the shot.
To me, the POV Head Tracker sounded like a dream accessory for shooting video solo — so I had to try it out for myself.
A game-changing accessory?
The IPX4-certified device measures just 1.0 x 1.0 x 0.5 inches and comes in a hard0shell USB-C battery case along with an ear mount, strap, clip, adhesive mount and motion adapter. It has has a 7-hour battery life — enough for a full day of shooting.
Insta360 also sent me a neck mount that's designed to hold the Luna Ultra. With the camera slotted into the neck mount and the POV Head Tracker in the supplied ear mount — which is right ear-only — I gave the combo a spin to see if it delivers on its lofty promises.
Setup takes a few seconds, via a simple device calibrate process: you look straight ahead for three seconds, then look straight down for three seconds. Done.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Once the devices are paired and calibrated, you control which way the camera points simply by where you look. Doing a hands-on product review? Look down at the product. Doing a travel vlog and the point of interest is off to the left? Look left. It really is that simple.
It really was like the camera was my second pair of eyes — and it's the biggest nod so far to Insta360 founder and CEO Liu Jingkang's 'photography robot' vision, which I spoke to both him and Insta360 about.
Is the POV Head Tracker perfect? I'm not so sure. It appears as though you can't use Insta360's Mic Pro simultaneously via Bluetooth, plus I found the tracker strayed off sync a little, and that slight difference was highlighted when employing the Luna Ultra's tighter 3x telephoto camera rather than the ultra-wide.
I needed to recalibrate the device from time to time (which can also be done by looking straight ahead and then double-tapping the Luna Ultra's button that recenters the camera).
Still, that's where the camera's detachable LCD screen module came in handy — you can leave the camera on the neck strap over your chest, but view what the camera sees on the detached module, for example if you do need to recalibrate or zoom.
The Luna Ultra with POV Head Tracker felt like a camera setup from the future. A future where people walk around with discreet cameras strapped to their chests, recording what they're looking at. Whether you want that future or not is another matter; but for now Insta360's new accessory feels like a revolutionary device.
It's another form of camera intelligence akin to the Luna Ultra's subject-tracking skills which, when combined with the detachable module, is like having a cameraperson filming you. These smart features make life for solo creators so much simpler, and broaden the range of shots possible.
The POV Head Tracker costs $69.99 / £67.99 / AU$115.99 while the Luna Ultra Neck Mount costs $24.99 / £23.99 / AU$39.99.

articles.title: Cómo cuidar la lengua de suegra en maceta en agosto 2026, según la IA
articles.text:
Cuidar una lengua de suegra en maceta puede ser sencillo si se tienen en cuenta algunas recomendaciones básicas.
Según la inteligencia artificial de Claude, los tres factores clave son la luz indirecta, el riego escaso y una maceta con buen drenaje.
En agosto, la temperatura en algunos países suele ser cálida, por lo que conviene ubicar la planta en un lugar donde no quede expuesta durante mucho tiempo al sol directo, y regarla solo cuando la tierra esté completamente seca.
PUBLICIDAD
Según Habibi Blog, un sitio dedicado a consejos de botánica, el sol directo moderado puede ser beneficioso: las variedades con bordes amarillos se vuelven más vibrantes con esa exposición.
Si en tu país agosto es un mes frío, procura que la planta no quede expuesta a corrientes de viento frío, ya que esto la reseca.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo cuidar una lengua de suegra en casa
La lengua de suegra (Dracaena trifasciata) es una de las plantas más resistentes y fáciles de cuidar en interiores. Originaria del oeste de África, tolera el olvido, la poca luz y el ambiente seco sin perder su porte elegante.
- Luz y ubicación
No necesita sol directo. Crece bien con luz indirecta, cerca de una ventana con cortina, aunque tolera espacios con poca iluminación como pasillos u oficinas.
PUBLICIDAD
Según Habibi Plantitas, un sitio especializado en botánica, las variedades con bordes amarillos ganan intensidad de color con sol moderado. Eso sí: evitá el sol directo del mediodía, que quema las hojas.
- Riego y sustrato.
El error más común es el exceso de agua. Se debe regar cada 10 y 15 días, solo cuando los primeros centímetros de tierra estén completamente secos. Usá una maceta con orificio de drenaje y sustrato ligero, idealmente mezcla para cactus o suculentas.
PUBLICIDAD
- Temperatura y cuidados generales.
Le sienta bien el clima cálido, entre 15 °C y 30 °C. No tolera heladas ni corrientes de viento frío.
De acuerdo con AD Magazine, purifica el aire al filtrar toxinas como el benceno y el formaldehído, y libera oxígeno incluso durante la noche, lo que la convierte en una opción ideal para dormitorios.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo cuidar una lengua de suegra con ayuda de la IA
Los usuarios que tienen una lengua de suegra o cualquier otra planta en casa pueden recurrir a la inteligencia artificial para resolver dudas sobre su estado, desde identificar enfermedades hasta recibir recomendaciones de riego y cuidado.
Plataformas como Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI y Grok permiten hacerle consultas al asistente virtual en lenguaje natural, como si se le preguntara a un experto.
PUBLICIDAD
El usuario puede escribir, por ejemplo, “las hojas de mi lengua de suegra se están poniendo amarillas” y recibir en segundos una explicación sobre las causas más probables y cómo resolverlas.
Pero la función más útil para los amantes de las plantas es la posibilidad de compartir fotos y videos directamente en el chat.
A partir de una imagen, estos sistemas pueden analizar el color de las hojas, detectar señales de pudrición, plagas o quemaduras por sol, y sugerir acciones concretas.
PUBLICIDAD
Algunos, como Gemini de Google o ChatGPT, procesan imágenes con un nivel de detalle que permite identificar problemas que a simple vista podrían pasar desapercibidos.
Las consultas más frecuentes incluyen con qué frecuencia regar según el clima de la ciudad, qué tipo de sustrato usar, cuándo trasplantar y cómo propagar la planta.
PUBLICIDAD
Es posible pedirle a la IA que elabore un calendario de cuidados personalizado según la época del año o las condiciones del hogar.
La lengua de suegra, conocida científicamente como Dracaena trifasciata, es una de las plantas de interior más resistentes que existen. Aun así, combinar su bajo mantenimiento con el asesoramiento de una IA puede marcar la diferencia entre una planta que sobrevive y una que prospera.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Epic Games tiene gratis Marvel Rivals y se une al estreno de la película Avengers: Doomsday
articles.text:
El estreno de Avengers: Doomsday está cada vez más cerca y, por eso, Epic Games ofrece gratis el juego Marvel Rivals para PC.
El título es un juego de disparos JcJ (jugador contra jugador) de superhéroes: reúne un equipo Marvel, combina sus poderes para idear estrategias y habilidades, y permite luchar en campos de batalla destruibles en constante cambio dentro del universo de Marvel.
PUBLICIDAD
Recientemente, la plataforma incorporó Path to Doomsday — Avengers: Age of Ultron, un nuevo modo JcE (jugador contra entorno) con escenas cinematográficas narrativas.
Cómo jugar gratis Marvel Rivals
Para obtener el Marvel Rivals sin costo, sigue estos pasos:

La licencia queda asociada a tu cuenta de forma permanente: no es necesario tenerlo instalado todo el tiempo para conservarlo.
Cómo acceder al modo de Avengers: Doomsday

- Abrir la pestaña Rivalidad y elegir Path to Doomsday: Avengers Age of Ultron.

Marvel Rivals es un juego de disparos JcJ (jugador contra jugador) de superhéroes desarrollado por NetEase Games. El jugador arma un equipo con personajes del universo Marvel, combina sus poderes para diseñar estrategias y combate en escenarios destruibles que cambian en tiempo real.

articles.title: Is bulldozing homes, seizing land, harming the climate, and replacing workers really worth everyone having an AI agent?
articles.text:
Is bulldozing homes, seizing land, harming the climate, and replacing workers really worth everyone having an AI agent?
AI agents will soon handle your work, and your personal life
There are a lot of sacrifices being made to usher in the latest technological age. Jobs, businesses, even whole industries are at risk of disappearing.
Now we can add homes to the list - as new electricity infrastructure for data centers in the state of Georgia means 30 homes are to be bulldozed and 330 parcels of land seized.
The good news is that the additional power will allow for extra data center capacity. And those same people who lost their houses can look forward to having their own personal AI agent to help to find a new place to live.
Losing homes for AI
In case you missed it, Mark Zuckerberg has announced yet another five year plan for AI, saying that billions of people will soon have their own personal AI agents - something that will require a data center buildout far beyond anything we’ve currently seen.
These agents will be “working on your behalf 24/7 to achieve your goals in whatever the domain is that you care about,” Zuckerberg said. They’ll basically do everything you already do, manage your relationships, sort your finances, even manage your household tasks.
So when AI frees everyone from the burdens of being human, what are we left to contend with? We get to channel the world's resources, climate, homes, and personal information and in return, AI can live your life for you. You’ll have so much free time to do… something else? Maybe listen to the tuneful hum of the local data center?
The promises of AI seem to add up to human replacement. The main reason businesses are chewing at the bit to adopt AI technology is because it promises to cut one of their main expenses: labor. The levels of productivity will stay the same, or maybe even improve, but profits will skyrocket thanks to significantly reduced operating costs.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
There will be new jobs in new never-before-thought-of sectors, or so we are told. But is this just a way to placate those losing their jobs to AI technology?
At present, AI is cutting through the entry level positions and administrative work that used to be a good way into a new industry. AI is therefore replacing existing workers, while simultaneously shutting them out from moving to other industries. Lets not forget that many workplaces are implementing AI interviewers that suck what was left of human interaction (much of which is a facade) out of the job seeking process.
As an added kick in the teeth, once you’ve lost your source of income your energy bills will likely rise as data centers attach to an already strained electricity grid. Many US electricity providers have upped bills as a way to pay for infrastructural upgrades to provide new connections for data centers. And don’t forget the air quality will get worse as more and more gas-burning turbines power up to meet the demand for power.
I still believe there is some good AI can do for the world, particularly in science and medicine. But the main benefit I expect AI to provide to the workplace is a revitalization of labor unions. Despite decades of union busting and a general decline in membership as the old guard retires, this new threat to workers will hopefully act as a catalyst to return labor unions to their former glory.
The more members they have, the stronger they are. No amount of AI agents can change that.

articles.title: 'It's a new era': I spoke to the passionate, ambitious, and visionary founders of Story Kitchen, who fought the videogame adaptation curse and Hollywood scepticism — and won
articles.text:
'That's our next mission — proving that games are art': meet Story Kitchen, the bold, trail-blazing studio behind the popular Sonic movies that wants to turn your favorite game into the next movie or TV hit
"It is easier, but it's not easy," Story Kitchen co-founder Dmitri Johnson interjects.
I'm midway through an in-depth conversation with Johnson and business partner Mike Goldberg about their pioneering entertainment company when the former clarifies something he alluded to earlier.
The topic in question? Pitching movies and TV shows based on video game properties to other studio figureheads is still challenging. That's in spite of myriad recent examples of popular game franchises being turned into other screen-based art forms that have achieved critical and commercial success.
"We're working every day to continue changing the stigma that games are only for kids and lazy people who still live in their mom's basement," Johnson adds with a wry smile. "These are artists and storytellers in their own right — and their work deserves to be seen by more people."
Press start
You probably haven't heard of Story Kitchen, but you definitely know the video game adaptations they've helped to shape.
From Paramount Pictures' money-spinning Sonic the Hedgehog film franchise and Netflix's animated Tomb Raider show, to Prime Video's forthcoming TV re-imaginings of the aforementioned Lara Croft-fronted game series and Dontnod's beloved first Life is Strange title, Story Kitchen is at the forefront of what's unsurprisingly being labeled the 'golden age' of video game adaptations.
It's a cinematic epoch some believed would never happen — and with good reason. The 1990s and early 2000s are littered with examples of maligned video game movies, including — but by no means limited to — 1993's The Super Mario Bros. Movie, 2005's Doom, and 2003's House of the Dead, the latter of which is one the worst-rated films on popular review aggregation website Rotten Tomatoes.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
With so many entertainment giants failing to understand the source material, the 'videogame adaptation curse' — a phrase Goldberg says "sounds really good when stories are written about it" — became a catch-all term for these and similarly crucified productions. Combine that with the notion that, as Goldberg notes, "Hollywood didn't respect the gaming community, developers, or publishers", and it seemed that video games would forever be viewed as the runt of the visual media landscape.
That was until dj2 Entertainment, the precursor to Story Kitchen co-founded by Johnson and Dan Jevons in 2011, took a leap into the unknown.
The company's primary goal was simple: make Hollywood believe that video game stories were worth telling and investing in. Predictably, Hollywood just didn't see the appeal of turning games into movies or TV shows, and countless rejections followed.
Then came the first Sonic the Hedgehog film. After slowly and methodically earning the trust and respect of SEGA, Johnson convinced the Japanese videogame titan and, later, Paramount Pictures that people wanted to see the Blue Blur star in his own movie.
A few notable setbacks, including the titular character's speedy redesign after fans attacked his initial look following the release of Sonic's first trailer, followed. Fast-forward to early 2020, though, and, despite the pandemic bringing Sonic the Hedgehog's theatrical run to a premature end, the action-adventure comedy grossed $320 million worldwide. On a reported budget of $90 million, it more than recouped its production and marketing costs.
"Dmitri always believed that, with education and respect, a different result [video game adaptations being successful] would occur," Goldberg says. "And, he was right."
'It's a new era — but not every game should be adapted'
A lot has happened in the short time since Sonic's big-screen debut, one that Goldberg describes as "an absolute game changer in the Hollywood ecosystem".
He's not wrong. Film adaptations of other iconic and/or hugely popular game series, including Mario and Minecraft, have earned billions at the global box office. Meanwhile, TV retellings of hit franchises like The Last of Us on HBO Max, and small-screen projects that expand on existing game universes, including Fallout on Prime Video and Netflix's League of Legends animated program Arcane, have drawn universal acclaim, won multiple awards, and introduced millions more people to stories, characters, and worlds they would never have connected with otherwise.
Suffice it to say, the explosion of video game adaptations is indicative of an industry-wide paradigm shift that also allowed dj2 Entertainment to level up its own game. Indeed, by investing the metaphorical skill points into the company's evolution from dj2 Entertainment to Story Kitchen, onboarding industry talents like Elena Sandoval and Timothy I. Stevenson, and signing first-look deals with Amazon in February 2022 and DreamWorks Animation in May 2024, Johnson, Goldberg, and company are well-placed to help create the next wave of gaming transmedia hits.
At the time of publication, around 30 projects, some of which have already found homes and others that'll be shopped around Hollywood, are in the works at Story Kitchen HQ. That might sound a lot, but it's a mere raindrop in the ever-expanding gaming ocean. So, why doesn't Story Kitchen just take a long list of game titles to film studios, TV networks, and the world's best streaming services, and reel them off until one piques their interest?
"It's a new era, but not every game should be adapted," Golberg replies, "And not every game should be adapted right now. We want to be a friend and advocate for the space, though, because we don't see this as a fleeting moment [for video game adaptations]. We think it's got long-term potential, so we're working to ensure that we see that through."
That's not to say Story Kitchen is only focused on adapting the biggest game franchises. AA and indie titles are as much a part of the pitching process, if not more so, than their flashier, big-budget counterparts.
"We don't go into things like 'how many copies did this game sell?'," Johnson says. "We actually despise that question and refuse to answer it at this point. We respond with 'here's why these characters and stories are incredible' and 'here's why it's something we've never seen before'.
"What it really boils down to is passion," he continues. "What are the things that we can't stop thinking about and have to pursue? Once that process starts, we're convinced something has to be made, and that translates into our meetings with other companies. Initially, it might not necessarily make sense to them, but they all want to hear the pitch because it's coming from a place of passion, so most networks and studios are excited when we take something out to them. This isn't a cash-grab — these conversations are happening because we actually care."
Prime-d for more success?
And care, Johnson and Goldberg certainly do. The multi-billion-dollar-spinning Sonic franchise, which currently comprises three movies and a Knuckles TV spin-off on Paramount+, has improved with each new entry.
As of July 2026, a fourth flick is deep in post-production ahead of its March 19, 2027 release date. An untitled Shadow-fronted off-shoot project is also reportedly in the works, though Johnson and Goldberg declined to speak about it because, as Goldberg rightfully points out, "there are levels of NDAs (non-disclosure agreements) we must respect."
Sonic the Hedgehog 4 isn't the only thing that'll roll off the Story Kitchen production line next year. Indeed, two TV projects are expected to make their Prime Video debuts in 2027, the first of which should be a Tomb Raider TV adaptation that Johnson admits has been "years in the making".
Overseen by Fleabag's Phoebe Waller-Bridge, it'll star Sophie Turner as gaming icon Lara Croft. Amazon revealed a perfect first-look shot at Turner in Croft's classic tank top and shorts combo as principal photography got underway in January and, while filming was halted in March due to a "minor injury" sustained by Turner, there's nothing to suggest it'll delay the live-action series' launch.
Thanks to a partnership Story Kitchen established with Tomb Raider custodians and videogame developer Crystal Dynamics during development on Netflix's Tomb Raider animated show, Johnson says "we had a very clear blueprint of how to move together as partners". So, when Amazon, which already had an agreement with Crystal Dynamics to publish future Tomb Raider games, proposed making a live-action TV show, it seemed like a lightning-in-a-bottle moment for all involved.
"Every decision [on the show] is made with Crystal Dynamics' sign-off," Johnson reveals. "So, season one has their blessing and they're very hands-on, but they also respect Phoebe, who's a super-fan, and her perspective of what a live-action Tomb Raider project should be.
"We've actually just started seeing rough cuts, and we were grinning like 10 year olds the entire time. It's going to be good. By the way, we're not the type of people who hype up their own s**t. It's going to be something that your mom can come across and not know that it's based on a 30-year-old videogame franchise. We don't want it to be a niche adaptation just for core fans, who we absolutely honor and will make feel seen. But, if we do our job right, which we're tirelessly trying to do, newcomers will fall love this show just as much as we have."
Life is Strange is a whole other beast. The 2015 episodic adventure game, which tells the story of a high schooler named Max who discovers she can rewind time, is famous for its branching dialog option-based narrative. Ultimately, though, the choices players make during any given playthrough lead to just one of two endings.
In collaboration with its production partners Amazon, Life is Strange franchise publisher Square Enix, and Margot Robbie's LuckyChap Entertainment, then, how is Story Kitchen tackling an evolving tale built on player choice? Furthermore, how did they decide which ending to not only use, but one that, regardless of what happens in Life is Strange: Reunion, aka Deck Nine's 2024 sequel to the first Max-led game, some viewers might interpret as being its true canonical ending?
"We went into Life is Strange knowing that almost all of the major decisions were almost a 50-50 split," Johnson muses. "So, at the start of development, you have to accept that you're not going to make everyone happy. That said, the way we're approaching some of those critical decisions from the games, I think everyone is are going to feel seen, and they're going to be happy and probably emotional [with how things play out]."
It's full steam ahead for Amazon MGM Studios film adaptations of two award-winning and popular Hazelight games in It Takes Two and Split Fiction, too.
Where the latter is concerned, things are still in the early stages of development. However, prolific actor Sydney Sweeney, Wicked duology director Jon M. Chi, and Deadpool writers Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick are, as confirmed by Goldberg, all involved.
"You play these games with your significant other, friend, or a family member, and everyone has their own experience," Goldberg says. It's been such a fun challenge of interpreting that and turning it into a singular shared experience [for viewers].
"Reese and Wernick even insisted on playing the game, and that's how we want our village to be built. You're not required to be a game, but we loved that they wanted to play and experience it together before they committed to this adaptation, and that's going to influence their own script."
As for It Takes Two's film reimagining, it's been over four years since Dwayne Johnson's Seven Bucks production team boarded the Amazon-led project. Speaking to Eurogamer last March, Hazelight creative director Josef Fares, who's known for not mincing his words, took aim at how long it was taking for the film to move forward.
"Hollywood, there's so much b******t," Fares responded when asked for an update. "I think 90 percent of the meetings are actually b******t, and 10 percent are what actually happens. There's a lot of talk, but not a lot of walk. I don't know what's going on. Hopefully something. It would be cool to get something out of it, but my hopes are not so high."
"They are," Johnson says when I ask him if Fares, Hazelight, and Johnson's company are still involved, before he adds: "We're so close to the Hazelight boys at this point that there's a shorthand with them, and the relationship with them and partners on our side... it's all very fluid."
Days of future past
That's just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the 30+ film and TV projects that Story Kitchen plans on delivering.
Johnson and Goldberg want to cover as many genre bases and demographics as possible, too. Film adaptations of three Roblox games — Grow a Garden, Steal a Brainrot, and Jailbreak — are in the works, as are Just Cause, Shinobi, and Ruiner productions with Universal.
Elsewhere, Netflix has signed on to bring Sifu and Kingmakers adaptations to its user base, Lionsgate is hard at work on a Streets of Rage movie, and film reimaginings of hit indie games Disco Elysium and Dredge have also been announced. Additionally, a House of the Dead movie led by The Last of Us and Superman star Isabela Merced — "she's our homie," Johnson beams —is just another of Story Kitchen's other planned projects.
It isn't just video games that are being turned into movies, either. Toys 'R Us, a popular toy retailer in the '80s and '90s that's recently enjoyed a resurgence in the US, is getting the live-action film treatment. Meanwhile, Teddy Ruxpin, an animatronic storytelling bear that was a US bestseller in the '80s, will star in a feature that's been described as 'Sonic the Hedgehog meets Elf'.
"I think it's going to go the same way as Barbie," self-confessed Teddy Ruxpin fan Johnson says in reference to the 2023 megahit starring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling. "I went into that thinking 'ugh, cash grab' and then had a little tear in the eye by the third act.
"It [the Teddy Ruxpin movie] is funnier than it has any right to be," Johnson continues. "We have ridiculous musical numbers when we shouldn't, and it's so brilliantly bananas that it works. I think it's going to catch people off-guard, and kids are gonna walk out of it wanting a Teddy Ruxpin."
But, back to the games — and, perhaps most importantly, Story Kitchen's mission to create films and TV shows not only based on beloved titles from the past and those that are currently popular, but also those yet to be released.
"We're about to pitch a show based on a game that hasn't even been announced," Goldberg teases as an example of the latter. "And, should nothing change, it'll finally be announced at the 2026 Game Awards. But we're already going to take a fully fleshed, packaged, and scripted drama TV pitch on it to studios next month, so we can move as swiftly as possible once the game is officially revealed."
Whatever that soon-to-be-announced game is, its developer will surely hope it performs as well as 2025 surprise hit Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 did.
The first-ever title from French studio Sandfall Interactive, Clair Obscur unexpectedly dominated the gaming sphere last year. With over eight million copies sold (as of April 2026) and numerous award wins under its belt, it's little wonder that this critically and commercially successful title is being turned into a live-action film. As Johnson is keen to point out, though, the Clair Obscur bandwagon isn't one that Story Kitchen jumped on post-launch.
"As a company, we pride ourselves on not chasing heat," he explains. "We're less likely to pursue a game once it's become an established hit, because we don't ever want to be seen as those people.
"We were actually working with Sandfall as early as 2023," he continues. "We read almost 600 pages of scripts, had raw music files [to listen to], [and] art to look at, so we fell in love with it before we saw any real gameplay. Obviously, you don't know how a game is going to perform, so we went into this knowing that it could be a tough sell. Without the massive success it had, it would've been an uphill battle [to pitch our movie adaptation to studios]. But, as I said earlier, once the passion kicks in, we don't take 'no' for an answer. We were convinced three years ago that this was something to be excited about, and... that's all we can say about it right now."
If there's one thing I took from my chat with Johnson and Goldberg, it's this: they genuinely care about what they're doing. Like, a lot. They don't phone in their work, nor did they lazily trot out stock responses to my questions. They are completely committed to telling the world that games are not only great, but that their stories are also worth translating and telling in other mediums.
There's so much more that Story Kitchen wants to accomplish, though. Even with the abundance of productions already on their plate, Johnson and Goldberg have ambitions on adapting even more franchises for the big and small screen. Their dream projects? Mega Man and — surprisingly — Bad Dudes for Johnson, and Nintendo's iconic sci-fi franchise Metroid for Goldberg.
But such wish fulfillment must wait for another day. As we approach the tail-end of what was supposed to be an hour-long interview, Goldberg reveals that he and Johnson are being summoned by Amazon for a meeting — the contents of which he can't disclose.
It's a sign of just how busy the pair have become, but they wouldn't have it any other way. After all, Story Kitchen is no ordinary passion project — it's reshaping the multimedia landscape as we know it.
"We were recently looking back on our list of games to consider for last year's BAFTA Game Awards," Johnson says, "And there's one from a tiny Australian team called The Drifter that, after I came across it in 2025, I couldn't stop gushing about. Anyway, we ended up tracking them down and, in the very first meeting we had with another studio, we were able to find a home for this indie game in the form of a big theatrical movie.
"That wouldn't have been possible five, six years ago, and that's why we're enjoying this moment now. Step one was getting rid of this silly notion that games are cursed. Now, step two, and we say this with a straight face, you'll see Oscars, Emmys, and BAFTAs being won by movies and TV shows that are based on games. That's our next mission: proving that videogames are art. The stories being told, the characters they contain... they're no different to a New York Times best-selling book — and we're ready to show the world why."

articles.title: Google retira el generador de imágenes de Google Earth: solo estuvo disponible 24 horas
articles.text:
Google retiró temporalmente el generador de imágenes con inteligencia artificial de Google Earth apenas 24 horas después de haber anunciado su disponibilidad global. La herramienta, impulsada por el modelo Nano Banana 2, permitía transformar las vistas satelitales mediante instrucciones escritas, pero la empresa decidió suspenderla tras detectar que podía utilizarse para crear imágenes falsas de lugares reales con potencial para la desinformación.
La función fue presentada oficialmente el 30 de julio de 2026 como una nueva capacidad de Google Earth orientada a la educación, la arquitectura, el urbanismo y la divulgación histórica.
PUBLICIDAD
Sin embargo, un día después, el 31 de julio, Google actualizó su anuncio para informar que revertía el lanzamiento mientras desarrolla medidas de protección más estrictas para evitar usos indebidos.
La compañía aclaró que la suspensión es temporal y que trabaja en nuevos controles antes de volver a poner la herramienta a disposición de los usuarios. Por el momento, no existe una fecha oficial para su regreso.
PUBLICIDAD
Una IA capaz de transformar cualquier lugar del planeta
La nueva función incorporaba el modelo de inteligencia artificial Nano Banana 2 dentro de la versión web de Google Earth. Su funcionamiento era sencillo: el usuario seleccionaba cualquier punto del mapa, activaba la opción para generar una imagen y escribía una descripción indicando cómo quería modificar ese lugar.
La inteligencia artificial utilizaba como base las imágenes satelitales, fotografías aéreas y modelos tridimensionales disponibles en Google Earth para crear nuevas representaciones visuales.
Google presentó la herramienta como una forma de enriquecer proyectos educativos y profesionales. Entre los ejemplos mencionados figuraban la reconstrucción visual de ciudades históricas como Pompeya, la elaboración de materiales didácticos sobre distintas épocas, la creación de infografías y la representación del aspecto futuro de edificios o desarrollos inmobiliarios antes de comenzar las obras.
PUBLICIDAD
Con esta tecnología, profesores, arquitectos, urbanistas y creadores de contenido podían generar ilustraciones más detalladas sin necesidad de utilizar programas especializados de diseño.
El problema apareció con escenas falsas sobre lugares reales
Aunque la herramienta estaba pensada para usos creativos, rápidamente comenzaron a aparecer ejemplos que evidenciaban su potencial para generar desinformación.
El investigador especializado en inteligencia de fuentes abiertas Henk van Ess realizó diversas pruebas en las que incorporó elementos completamente ficticios sobre ubicaciones reales. Entre ellas aparecían una supuesta planta nuclear, un accidente de tráfico y escenarios con daños asociados a conflictos.
PUBLICIDAD
Posteriormente, el medio especializado 404 Media recopiló estos experimentos y advirtió que las imágenes podían difundirse fuera de contexto, dando la impresión de representar acontecimientos reales.
El principal riesgo no residía únicamente en la generación del contenido, sino en la facilidad con la que esas imágenes podían compartirse en redes sociales, aplicaciones de mensajería o plataformas digitales sin explicar que habían sido creadas mediante inteligencia artificial.
PUBLICIDAD
Google asegura que nunca modificó los mapas originales
Tras anunciar la suspensión, Google explicó que la función nunca alteró el contenido oficial de Google Earth.
Las imágenes creadas por la IA eran archivos independientes generados para cada usuario y no reemplazaban las fotografías satelitales ni los modelos tridimensionales visibles para el resto de las personas.
PUBLICIDAD
Asimismo, la empresa indicó que cada imagen incorporaba una marca destinada a identificar su origen artificial.
Sin embargo, Google reconoció que algunos usuarios compartieron capturas que aparentemente incumplían sus políticas de uso. Esa situación llevó a la compañía a detener el despliegue mientras desarrolla mecanismos adicionales para reducir el riesgo de abuso.
PUBLICIDAD
Las limitaciones de las marcas de agua
Uno de los desafíos más importantes para este tipo de herramientas es que las señales que identifican una imagen generada por IA pueden perder eficacia una vez que el contenido sale de la plataforma.
Una captura de pantalla, un recorte o una nueva compresión de la imagen pueden eliminar o dificultar la visualización de esas marcas, haciendo más complicado distinguir una recreación artificial de una fotografía auténtica.
PUBLICIDAD
En consecuencia, una escena completamente inventada podría circular por internet como si mostrara un hecho real, especialmente cuando representa lugares conocidos o acontecimientos de actualidad.
Este tipo de situaciones preocupa cada vez más tanto a empresas tecnológicas como a investigadores dedicados al estudio de la desinformación digital.
Google busca reforzar las protecciones antes de reactivar la función
La retirada del generador de imágenes evidencia el reto que enfrentan las compañías tecnológicas al incorporar inteligencia artificial generativa en productos utilizados por millones de personas.
Por un lado, estas herramientas ofrecen nuevas posibilidades para la educación, el diseño, la arquitectura y la creación de contenido. Por otro, también pueden facilitar la elaboración de imágenes falsas cada vez más convincentes cuando se combinan con escenarios reales.
Google no detalló qué cambios implementará antes de reactivar la función ni cuánto tiempo permanecerá deshabilitada. Su comunicación únicamente señala que el objetivo es desarrollar barreras más sólidas que impidan la generación y difusión de contenido que vulnere sus políticas.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Plug-in batteries will be the next ‘game changer’ for home energy, experts predict — here’s why they’ll be ‘bigger than solar’ and could save you up to £400 a year
articles.text:
‘Plug-in batteries are the real game-changer’: I talked to Octopus Energy and Anker about the home energy revolution than could soon be 'bigger than solar' for millions
The next 'air fryer' moment? Don't bet against it
It's typical, you wait for ages for a home energy revolution and then two come along at once — or at least that's what appears to be happening in the UK.
You've probably heard about the first landmark moment. 'Plug-in solar' hit the headlines last week when the UK government announced that small, solar panel kits that feed electricity directly into your standard home socket can legally go on sale from August 27.
That's a big deal. Plug-in solar means that millions of people who have traditionally been locked out of generating their own clean electricity — renters and flat owners, for example — will be able to join the residential solar party, albeit on a more modest scale.
But not everyone was celebrating wildly with biodegradable confetti. Across the country, energy nerds bemoaned one glaring omission in the government's new legislation — a legal pathway for 'plug-in batteries'.
For many, these small home batteries — think a mini Tesla Powerwall that plugs into a standard wall socket — are the "real game-changer", as Octopus Energy and Anker both described them to me. That's because they promise to be even more accessible than plug-in solar and act as a money-saving brain that makes your home an active part of a smarter UK electricity grid.
Bold claims indeed, so I spoke to four of the biggest players in this burgeoning space — Anker, Octopus Energy, EcoFlow and Windfall Energy — along with the UK government to find out when plug-in batteries might be coming, what the drawbacks are and, most importantly, how much you can really expect to save...
When are they coming?
The main premise of plug-in home batteries, like the Windfall Battery above, is simple — they charge automatically using cheap-rate electricity (usually at night), then discharge that electricity around your home during more expensive peak-rate periods. "Even without solar panels, a plug-in battery delivers meaningful savings through grid arbitrage alone," Anker Solix's EU CEO, Kelvin Cao, tells me. Savings estimates range from between £100-£400 per year, depending on your battery, tariff and usage.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Great, so when exactly will they become legal in the UK? When I asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), the official answer was predictably vague. "We are rolling out plug-in solar, which will be quickest to reach the market — helping to bring bills down for good," a DESNZ spokesperson said.
Plug-in batteries are smart energy storage devices that connect to your home's electrical network through a standard wall socket, without any professional installation. They automatically charge from the grid when electricity is cheap and release energy back into your home during peak-rate hours to cut your energy bills. They can work on their own or alongside solar. While they're not currently legal in the UK, that could potentially change soon.
The DESNZ told me its main focus right now is plug-in solar kits and that plug-in batteries have their own technical and regulatory hurdles, which it's currently investigating. Still, there are hopes that grid-connected batteries that plug into your wall socket could be legalised within the next year.
Several big players are quietly preparing plug-in batteries — which are already available in countries like Germany — for a UK launch. Anker, for example, has built a page for its Solix Solarbank 4 that clearly explains the benefits of plug-in batteries, should they become legalised in the UK. "We are eager to support the rise of the plug-in era in the UK and become part of its evolving energy landscape," Anker Solix's EU CEO, Kelvin Cao, told me.
Octopus Energy also recently announced that its new plug-in Nook Cube battery will go on sale sometime in 2027. More confident on the timescale is Windfall Energy, a London startup that's designed the best-looking piece of home energy kit I've seen for a while, the Windfall Battery.
"I was at a roundtable with a Minister of Parliament about a month ago, and everyone there was pretty much calling for batteries to come hot on the heels of plug-in solar," Windfall Energy's co-founder Rob Hallifax told me.
So when is Windfall expecting to start selling its 2.5 kWh home battery, which has an RRP of £1,200 and had previously been slated to ship in autumn? "Winter is more likely now. We want to time it with the plug-in regulations. It’s looking like the end of this year, early next," he added.
Why now?
You'll probably have noticed that the UK has been on an energy rollercoaster that can technically be described as 'not fun'.
Back in the late 1990s and early 2000s, inflation-adjusted gas and electricity prices were actually stable or even falling. But there was a huge spike for both in early 2022 and they've never returned to pre-energy crisis levels. Electricity prices are still 13% higher than in January 2020, according to the UK government, and they continue to move in the wrong direction.
Plug-in batteries promise to be, if not a cure, then at least a much-needed pain killer for our energy bills headache. They're emerging now because of three things — falling prices for lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries, the easing of electrical regulations in some regions (Germany created the world's first dedicated plug-in solar product standard in late 2025), and soaring wholesale gas prices that are reflected in the graph above.
As Anker's Kelvin Cao tells me, this has "reshaped how European households think about electricity". Unfortunately, that double-digit increase in energy prices is also "unlikely to come down any time soon". That's why Germany started the trend, and the UK is (hopefully) about to follow.
So how exactly do plug-in batteries save you money? "There’s two parts to the price saving," Windfall Energy's co-founder Rob Hallifax tells me. "The simple one is just the price arbitrage. So if you're paying 10p at night and 30p in the day for electricity per kilowatt hour, then you buy it at 10p, use it when it's 30p, you're saving 20p per kilowatt hour," he says.
That part's pretty simple — with the Windfall Battery, this 'buy low, use when prices skyrocket' approach makes up about £168 of its promised £250 per year savings. But there are also extra savings from getting your plug-in battery really singing in tune with the electricity network.
The UK grid acts a bit like a giant smart thermostat, signaling when the system needs more or less electricity, and the idea is that energy suppliers could follow by telling plug-in home batteries when to charge and discharge. Smaller plug-in batteries would likely be capped at an 800W output (without professional installation), so wouldn't be exporting power to the grid. But they could still play a role in balancing demand.
This makes tariffs the second big factor in the money-saving potential of plug-in batteries — and that's something Octopus Energy has been a UK leader in.
"The energy sector overall has not really embraced the fact that you can just offer different types of products to different types of consumer customer groups," Alex Schoch, Group Director for Flexibility at Octopus Energy, tells me. "Of our eight million customers, 1.2 million are on some kind of smart tariff," he adds.
Octopus Energy told me there could potentially be dedicated plug-in battery tariffs or bolt-ons for existing ones. If you've ever been baffled by choosing the right energy tariff, this could also get simpler thanks to plug-in batteries.
"I equate it to the evolution of mobile phone plans," Octopus Energy's Alex Schoch tells me. "First, they were incredibly generic. Then they got so complicated that Carphone Warehouse came into being just to explain the complexity. And now we’re at a stage where we create hyper-personalised plans based on your needs as a consumer. We’re on that same journey when it comes to energy".
But doesn't this also demand a lot of trust in energy companies? Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax agrees, but thinks falling bills will ultimately convince consumers. "It's their (consumers'] battery, they're in control of it, but the energy company is controlling it a bit to help them maximize the savings," he says. "The consumer has to trust that the energy company is doing this to save them money, and I think that will come when they see their bills go down," he adds.
What's the catch?
Clearly, plug-in batteries won't be a magic wand for everyone's bills, even if the batteries could be subsidised or even given away for free by the UK government to lower-income households, as the i Paper reported recently (the DESNZ declined to comment on this when I asked).
For most plug-in batteries, the payback period (the time it takes for savings to cover the cost of the battery) is expected to be around 3-4 for years, so not exactly a financial quick fix. The Windfall Battery promises annual savings of £250 (with an RRP of £1,200), while Anker tells me that the larger Solix Solarbank 4 on a dynamic tariff like Octopus Agile could save you just under £400 per year. That battery has no UK price yet, but retails for €1,999 in Europe (around £1,700).
The other concern raised by skeptics is safety. Is allowing potentially millions of households to connect batteries to their electricity networks without professional installation really a good idea? Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax acknowledges that it's an understandable concern. "People see a battery, and they think of scooters and fires, and there some valid concerns. Obviously, safety is critically important, and just one battery fire would be one too many," he says.
"But modern batteries are generally extremely safe,' he adds. "There are some studies out of Germany now where they compare batteries to EVs and other home appliances. One headline is that they’re typically about as safe as a washing machine," he adds. The other common comparison is with fan heaters, which are legal in the UK but carry a higher risk of 'user error' incidents than plug-in batteries.
Still, the added complexities of grid-charging batteries mean some agree with the UK government's top-dipping approach. EcoFlow, one of the biggest global players in home batteries, is among them. "We're aware and completely understand that these things take time," Lorna Wallace-Smith (EcoFlow's Head of UK PR) told me. "The fact that they were able to move forward with at least one step is is great" she added.
But hasn't Germany's rapid adoption of both plug-in solar and home batteries shown it's safe? "I think that's something we should learn from, as well as not fast-track into something without knowing it's absolutely built for UK homes," she added.
Could they outshine solar?
Despite these concerns, it seems clear that plug-in batteries have the potential to eclipse the more complex plug-in solar kits in the UK — and most of the experts I spoke to agreed.
"They are the fundamental great equalizer," says Octopus' Alex Schoch on plug-in batteries. "It’s such an important thing for renters because you can then take it with you to your next place," he adds.
"I think in the next couple of years we will see plug-in batteries really be the transformational scale deployment. I think it has the potential of being a mass market thing even faster than solar," he predicts.
Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax naturally agrees when comparing plug-in batteries to their solar equivalent. "There are 28 million homes in the UK and about half of them are either rented or flats and small homes. So more people could get them, millions, and there’s also the benefit to the grid and to the system," he says.
There is one other obvious comparison with an accessory that's cheap, easy to use and promises to save you money. "We use air fryers as quite a good example. Four or five years ago they just came from nowhere and suddenly half the country has one," he says.
But wouldn't an 'air fryer' level of popularity also cause a problem for plug-in batteries? After all, a lot of their money-saving potential comes from tapping into today's so-called 'delta' between cheap-rate and peak-rate electricity. If plug-in batteries help to solve the imbalance of today's grid demand — and tariffs are adjusted to reflect that — could that start to diminish their savings potential?
"I think yes and no," says Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax. "So maybe in 50 years the whole grid will be sort of perfect. I think the fundamental thing is that if you have renewable generation, that's always going to be variable. That's just the nature of the world. And so somewhere in the system, storage has to be part of it," he adds.
Octopus Energy's Alex Schoch agrees that such a change would be a long way off. "In theory, yes." he says in response to my pessimistic scenario. "But I would actually say the length of time here is measured in decades, not in a sub-decade quantum," he adds.
However, he does note that a similar process is already happening. "We've had such an explosion of solar in the UK over the last few years that now during Spring and Summer, a lot of the cheapest wholesale price electricity times are actually late morning, early afternoon, mid afternoon, and no longer overnight," he notes.
Charging ahead
The legalisation of plug-in batteries in the UK appears to be a matter of 'when' not 'if'. As a flat owner in south west London with no roof and only a limited appetite for plug-in solar, I'm right in the target market — and will certainly be interested when that moment comes.
But it also won't be an impulse buy where I snap up the first thing I see Amazon. "The biggest pitfall to avoid is making decision on price alone," says Anker's Kelvin Cao. "Now that plug-in solar has regulatory approval, the UK market will attract a wave of low-cost imports, some of which will be excellent and some of which will not. This will be a similar problem once the plug-in batteries are legalised," he warns.
"A battery that cuts corners on cell quality, protective engineering and compliance with applicable safety standards might look more attractive on its price tag, but it will not deliver the same reliability over the 10 to 15 years that a household should reasonably expect," he adds. In other words, buying cheap could backfire when it comes to savings.
So what exactly should you look for when plug-in batteries are legalised? "As a baseline, consumers should look for durable LFP battery cells, a high cycle life, robust protection against weather and corrosion, and integrated safeguards against electrical and thermal risks," Kelvin Cao says.
"They'll probably also say that the product must be listed on the Energy Networks Association (ENA) Type Test Register to demonstrate that its protection settings meet G98 requirements," adds Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax.
A real-world view
A large number of early adopters are already getting a taste of the benefits of a battery-only setup. One of those is TechRadar contributor Mark Pickavance, who wrote our EcoFlow Stream Ultra X review (which is well worth a read).
I caught up with him to see how it's going and he continues to be impressed. He told me that his monthly energy costs are down by about £40 a month with his setup (which was installed with the help of an electrician), and you could get most of that from a single Ultra X.
The only problem is that this stuff can get addictive. "I started with the premise of using just a battery, but once you have one the logical progression is solar. However, for people renting, it's the ideal solution, and if you use an Economy 7-like tariff (Octopus Go), you can take a chunk out of your costs," he said.
The arrival of plug-in solar from August could, then, be a good dry run of what to expect when plug-in batteries arrive. The big differences between residential buildings between Germany and the UK could mean plug-in solar doesn't quite take off in the same way in the UK, but Anker's Kelvin Cao remains bullish.
"This is no longer a niche movement. Germany passed one million officially registered plug-in solar systems in 2025, with around 430,000 new systems registered during that year alone," he notes. If plug-in batteries follow a similar pattern in the UK, that could have big consequences for energy bills — and the UK's grid as a whole.

Mark is TechRadar's Senior news editor. Having worked in tech journalism for a ludicrous 17 years, Mark is now attempting to break the world record for the number of camera bags hoarded by one person. He was previously Cameras Editor at both TechRadar and Trusted Reviews, Acting editor on Stuff.tv, as well as Features editor and Reviews editor on Stuff magazine. As a freelancer, he's contributed to titles including The Sunday Times, FourFourTwo and Arena. And in a former life, he also won The Daily Telegraph's Young Sportswriter of the Year. But that was before he discovered the strange joys of getting up at 4am for a photo shoot in London's Square Mile.
